instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek with Kiowa and Comanche, 1867-10-21
summary: The author annotates Medicine Lodge articles 6-10, 11 (railroad, emigrant and military-post clauses), 13, 14 and 16 against the council transcripts and says these terms were never discussed with tribal leaders. He calls the treaty contents fabrications of the commissioners and their staff.
verbatim_quote: The contents of this treaty are all fabrications by the US commissioners and their staff. None of this is in the treaty transcripts.
sources_cited_by_source: Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission of 1867-68 (DeMallie & Deloria 1975) cited for the transcripts (endnotes 12-14, earlier chunk)
federal_account_contrast: Kappler prints the articles as the agreed text. PSL says only the hunting right (Art. 11) was actually discussed, so most of the text was not consented to.
map_implication: Flag the 1867 KCA treaty record: 'articles largely absent from council transcripts per PSL'; do not imply informed consent to allotment, school, railroad or military-post clauses.
notes: These are the author's commentary. A side-by-side check against the published proceedings is needed to confirm article by article. The Art. 6 note says it 'was not in the documented proceedings.'

place: Lands south of the Arkansas River; old Little Arkansas reservation
instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek with Kiowa and Comanche, 1867-10-21 Art. 11 and 16
summary: Article 11 kept the right to hunt on any lands south of the Arkansas River 'so long as the buffalo may range thereon', and barred white settlement on the old 1865 reservation for three years. PSL says this was hollow because the military was killing buffalo at the same time to force the tribes onto reservations.
verbatim_quote: This was a hollow promise as the military at this time was killing buffalo to force the Indians onto reservations.
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text (RIT 364, 15 Stat. 581)
federal_account_contrast: The federal record treats the hunting right as a reserved right that simply lapsed. PSL frames its ending as deliberate destruction of the resource.
map_implication: Map the Art. 11 reserved hunting area (lands south of the Arkansas, incl. SE Colorado) as a reserved-use right, not plain ceded land; note the old 1865 reservation's 3-year no-settlement clause.
notes: The text notes that part of Art. 11 appears in pencil in the original, and gives transcription notes (asterisks) on the original treaty.

instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek with Kiowa and Comanche, 1867-10-21 Art. 15
summary: Article 15 gave $750 for a house for Comanche chief Tosh-e-wa (Silver Brooch) and $500 a year in presents to the ten best farmers. PSL says this should be treated as an illegal bribe.
verbatim_quote: Without question, this needs to be considered illegal and a bribe.
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text
federal_account_contrast: Kappler frames this as an incentive provision.
map_implication: Annotate the 1867 treaty with the Art. 15 payment to an individual chief as an alleged inducement.
notes: The characterization as bribery is the author's opinion; the payment itself is in the treaty text.

instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek with Kiowa and Comanche, 1867-10-21 Art. 12
summary: Article 12 made any cession of the common reservation invalid unless signed by at least three-fourths of the adult male Indians occupying it. PSL says the government was never able to get three-fourths of adult males to sign a change.
verbatim_quote: unless executed and signed by at least three-fourths of all the adult male Indians occupying the same
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text
federal_account_contrast: This is the treaty's own consent rule. The later 1892/1900 cession did not meet it, according to PSL and Clark.
map_implication: Store the Art. 12 three-fourths consent rule as a property of the 1867 KCA reservation; any later cession record should be tested against it.
notes: Note the treaty text cross-references 'Article III [VI]' for individual selections.

summary: PSL says the Jerome Commission 'supposedly' got 456 signatures out of 562 adult males, which would be 81 percent and above the Article 12 three-fourths threshold. Many people said they did not sign or were deceived. Opposition leader A'piatan accused the commission of fraud. PSL says the commission 'coerced' the tribes.
verbatim_quote: The commission supposedly obtained 456 signatures from among the 562 males to more than meet the three-fourths requirement of the 1867 Medicine Lodge Treaty.
sources_cited_by_source: Kansas Historical Society, Kansapedia 'Kiowa' (endnote 16)
federal_account_contrast: The federal record treats the agreement as carrying the required three-fourths. PSL disputes the count and the way signatures were gathered.
map_implication: Flag the 1892 Jerome Agreement cession of the KCA reservation as 'contested signature count; alleged fraud and deception'.
notes: 456/562 = 81.1 percent, so the claimed count passes 75 percent only if every signature is valid; the dispute is about validity. Clark (p.67) says it 'did not contain sufficient signatures, even with forgeries'.

instrument: Jerome Agreement as modified by Act of June 6, 1900
summary: Quoting C. Blue Clark (Encyclopedia of the Great Plains), the report says Congress in 1900 approved a modified agreement that lacked enough signatures even counting forgeries.
verbatim_quote: In 1900 Congress had approved a modified 1892 allotment agreement that did not contain sufficient signatures, even with forgeries
sources_cited_by_source: Blue Clark, C., 2011, 'Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock', Encyclopedia of the Great Plains, egp.law.027 (endnote 17)
federal_account_contrast: Statutes at Large present the 1900 act as ratifying a tribal agreement. Clark says the signatures were insufficient and included forgeries.
map_implication: Mark the 1900 KCA cession as 'ratified despite insufficient signatures incl. forgeries (Clark)'; do not render as consensual cession.
notes: Clark's count claim conflicts with the 456/562 figure on p.66; both appear in the source.

instrument_cite: 31 Stat. 677; S. Misc. Doc. No. 102, 53rd Cong., 2nd Sess. (1893)
summary: Congress sat on the 1892 agreement for eight years and then passed an altered version in which almost every article was changed. The changes were never taken back to the tribes. PSL says cattle owners and landgrabbers drove the changes and that the alterations should be considered fraud.
verbatim_quote: When the Jerome Commission's agreement was finally passed, the document had been altered, and almost every article was changed. The changes were never taken back to the Tribes for approval.
sources_cited_by_source: Act of June 6, 1900, 31 Stat. 677 (endnote 32); S. Misc. Doc. No. 102 (1893) (endnote 33); endnote 34 text missing from chunk
federal_account_contrast: The statute appears as ratification of a negotiated agreement. PSL says Congress changed it on its own, without the tribes' consent.
map_implication: Tag the 1900 act as 'Congress-amended agreement never re-submitted to tribes'.
notes: Endnotes 34-45 are not in this chunk (p.78 blank), so the specific source for 'should have been considered fraud' and the ICC docket notes is unavailable here.

summary: During the eight years before ratification, thousands of settlers illegally rushed onto Kiowa lands, took stone, timber and minerals, and set up farms. Towns grew as the Rock Island Railroad was built through the north of the reservation.
verbatim_quote: During that time, thousands of Euro-American settlers illegally rushed into Kiowa lands. These settlers robbed the reservation's stone, timber, and minerals while establishing farms.
sources_cited_by_source: Kansas Historical Society, Kansapedia 'Kiowa' (endnote 16)
federal_account_contrast: Adds illegal pre-ratification occupation that the cession record does not show.
map_implication: Note pre-1900 illegal settlement and resource theft on the KCA reservation.

instrument: Jerome Agreement vs Medicine Lodge Art. 6
summary: The commission offered 160-acre allotments although Medicine Lodge had provided up to 320 acres per head of family if the land were divided.
verbatim_quote: The commission proposed that the land be divided into 160-acre plots, but the Medicine Lodge Treaty of 1867 called for 320-acre plots
sources_cited_by_source: Kansapedia 'Kiowa'
federal_account_contrast: Shows the allotment terms cut the treaty's individual land guarantee in half.
map_implication: Note the reduction from 320-acre treaty selections to 160-acre allotments.
notes: Art. 6 actually says 'not exceeding' 320 acres for a head of family and 80 for single adults over 18.

summary: Lone Wolf sued Interior Secretary Ethan A. Hitchcock to stop allotment. The Supreme Court ruled in 1903 that Congress has plenary power and can abrogate treaty rights, and that its motives cannot be reviewed. The Art. 12 three-fourths condition was sidestepped. The surplus was quickly opened to settlers.
verbatim_quote: Kiowa claims, including the condition of article 12 of the Medicine Lodge Treaty (1867) forbidding cession of Indian land unless approved by three-fourths of the tribe's male members, were sidestepped in the Court's opinion.
sources_cited_by_source: Blue Clark 2011 (endnote 17); Echo-Hawk 2013, In the Light of Justice, 178 (endnote 18); Kansapedia
federal_account_contrast: The federal legal record treats the cession as valid under plenary power. The source frames the case as legalizing a treaty breach.
map_implication: Link the KCA surplus land opening (1901) to Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock as 'cession upheld without valid tribal consent'.
notes: The source gives no U.S. Reports cite (187 U.S. 553 is the standard cite; not in source). Day not stated in the source.

summary: More than 50,000 settlers took the tribal land. Allotment ran 1906-1936. Over 65 percent of individual Kiowa holdings and about 93 percent of tribal pasture lands were lost. Oil and gas leases from 1914 paid little and were controlled by the government.
verbatim_quote: Over 65 percent of individual tribal land holdings were lost to Euro-American settlers, and roughly 93 percent of tribal-owned pasture lands were lost.
sources_cited_by_source: Kansapedia 'Kiowa' (endnote 19)
federal_account_contrast: Adds what happened after cession to the land that was reserved.
map_implication: Annotate the KCA reservation with the post-allotment loss figures (65% individual, 93% pasture).
notes: The text says 'southeastern Oklahoma'; the KCA reservation was in southwestern Oklahoma, so this is likely a slip in the source.

summary: The government argued that any award for the Jerome Agreement should be offset by $1.5 million in depredation damages charged to the tribe. The ICC rejected depredation offsets as contrary to the purpose of the proceedings. Kansapedia says the Kiowa were awarded nearly $2 million in 1960 after 11 years.
verbatim_quote: The Indian Claims Commission resolved that offsets for depredations were contrary to the purpose of the proceedings.
sources_cited_by_source: Kansapedia 'Kiowa' (endnote 27)
federal_account_contrast: Shows the government tried to charge the tribe for 'depredations' against the award.
map_implication: In ICC data, record the proposed $1.5M depredation offset (rejected).
notes: The 'nearly $2 million in 1960' figure does not match the Docket 32 dates below (Amended Final Award 1957-03-29, $2,067,166). Needs checking.

instrument: ICC Docket No. 32 (Kiowa, Comanche, and Apache Tribes v. United States)
instrument_cite: ICC Docket 32; 1 Ind. Cl. Comm. 505; Act of June 6, 1900, 31 Stat. 677
summary: The tribes claimed $16,268,664. The ICC found the land 'unconscionably' acquired (1951-04-09). Additional Findings (1955-12-13) set the ceded area at 2,033,583 acres worth $4,067,166 ($2.00 per acre) as of 1900-06-06, minus the $2,000,000 already paid. The final award was $2,067,166. The government appealed and lost; the Amended Final Award came on 1957-03-29, with no 5% compound interest and no land returned.
verbatim_quote: concluded that the ceded area consisted of 2,033,583 acres, with a fair market value of $4,067,166 as of June 6, 1900
sources_cited_by_source: ICC 1951a/b Docket 32, 1 Ind. Cl. Comm. 505, Findings of Fact and Opinion; Additional Findings of Fact 1955-12-13 (endnotes 28-29)
federal_account_contrast: Royce and Kappler show a cession. The ICC itself found it unconscionable and paid $2/acre, and nearby land was selling at up to $11/acre.
map_implication: For the 1900 KCA cession polygon: claimed $16,268,664; award $2,067,166 net (gross $4,067,166 less $2,000,000 offset); 2,033,583 acres; valued at $2.00/acre; no land returned.
notes: The source says the government appeal went to the 'Court of Federal Claims' (then the Court of Claims). The 1955 date sits in endnote 28's citation.

summary: Section 22 makes payment a full discharge of all claims and bars any further claim. PSL says the government could appeal awards (and did) while the tribes' reservation of appeal rights was automatically barred, which it calls discriminatory.
verbatim_quote: payment of any claim, after a determination under the Act, shall be a full discharge of the United States of all claims and demands touching any of the matters involved
sources_cited_by_source: ICC Act Sec. 22 (endnote 35, text missing in chunk); TREC rec. endnote 8
federal_account_contrast: The federal framing is that ICC payment extinguishes title. PSL treats it as payment-as-extinguishment without consent.
map_implication: For every KCA polygon resolved through the ICC, label 'extinguished by ICC payment (Sec. 22), not by land return'.

place: NW Texas, W Kansas, SE Colorado, (Oklahoma panhandle area)
instrument: ICC Dockets 257 and 259-A; Treaty of Little Arkansas with Kiowa and Comanche 1865-10-18
instrument_cite: ICC Docket 257, 26 Ind. Cl. Comm. 101 (1971-08-09); Docket 259-A; RIT 343, 14 Stat. 717
summary: The ICC granted summary judgment that the tribes held 'recognized title' under the 1865 Little Arkansas treaty to about 39,680,000 acres (Royce areas 510 and 511, map 57) in NW Texas, W Kansas and SE Colorado. After a commissioner's dissent and a Court of Claims referral back, the final judgment awarded $35,060,000, fully approved 1974-04-17. PSL calls it the largest ICC award ever.
verbatim_quote: This tract of land contained approximately 39,680,000 acres located in the northwestern part of the present state of Texas, the western portion of Kansas, the southeastern corner of Colorado
sources_cited_by_source: ICC Docket 257, 26 Ind. Cl. Comm. 101, 123-131 (endnote 5); RIT 343, 14 Stat. 717 (endnote 4); endnotes 37-42 missing from chunk
federal_account_contrast: Royce 510/511 appear as ceded by the 1867 treaty. The ICC found recognized title, so money, not land, closed the claim.
map_implication: Royce 510 and 511: tag 'recognized title (ICC Dockets 257/259-A); taken via 1867 treaty; compensated $35,060,000 in 1974 with no land returned'. Treat the SE Colorado portion as KCA treaty-recognized land.
notes: The 'largest ever ICC award' claim needs checking. The government's res judicata argument was rejected. PSL calls the 1867 commission a 'war and relocation commission'.

summary: PSL argues the awards were negligible: no land returned, no 5% compound interest (which PSL says would make $35M worth over $12 billion), no accounting for buffalo loss (put at $48 billion), and no trespass damages under the 1834 Trade and Intercourse Act's $1,000 fine. It says the tribes got $1.00 per acre while nearby land sold for $11.00.
verbatim_quote: the settlement was negligible when juxtaposed against the value of other land in the area being sold for $11.00 per acre while the tribes received $1.00 an acre
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 43-44 (missing from chunk); 1834 Trade and Intercourse Act
federal_account_contrast: This is a critique of ICC valuation methods.
map_implication: In ICC tooltips, show the per-acre award next to contemporary market value where it is known.
notes: Internal inconsistencies: $1.00/acre here vs $2.00/acre for Docket 32 (p.72); buffalo value $48B (p.74) vs $46B (p.92 endnote 11). $35,060,000 / 39,680,000 acres is about $0.88/acre. The $12B interest figure is not shown with any working.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Atkinson with Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, 1853-07-27
summary: The Fort Atkinson treaty allowed US forts and protected emigrant trails in exchange for $18,000 per year to the signing tribes. Plains Apache headmen Poor Wolf, Poor Bear, Prairie Wolf and Cigar signed.
verbatim_quote: the sum of eighteen thousand dollars per annum
sources_cited_by_source: Avalon Project text of Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, July 27, 1853 (endnote 9)
federal_account_contrast: Names Plains Apache signers who are often merged with the Kiowa.
map_implication: List the Plains Apache signers on the 1853 Fort Atkinson treaty record.
notes: The text says 'By 1850 and 1855' and 'ratified on July 27, 1853'; July 27, 1853 is the signing date. Category ANNUITY_THEFT is not established for this treaty in the chunk; it is used only for the annuity promise. Reviewer may prefer OTHER.

place: Rocky Mountains; Front Range; SE Colorado; Arkansas Valley
summary: PSL says the Kiowa Apache have historical ties to the Rocky Mountains, the Front Range and SE Colorado, and share in the Medicine Lodge annuities and in the acknowledgment of territorial claims with the Kiowa and Comanche. It warns that their history risks being erased by merging it into other nations' histories.
verbatim_quote: In terms of the territorial claims in Colorado, the Kiowa Apache have historical ties to the Rocky Mountains, the Front Range, and the southeastern part of the state.
sources_cited_by_source: No specific cite for this sentence
federal_account_contrast: Royce and Kappler usually fold the Apache into the KCA or Cheyenne-Arapaho entries.
map_implication: Show the Apache Tribe of Oklahoma as a distinct nation linked to SE Colorado, Front Range and Arkansas Valley areas, not only as part of 'Kiowa'.

place: First Battle of Adobe Walls, northern Texas panhandle
summary: Kit Carson's troops attacked a Kiowa and Comanche village. The Kiowa Apache suffered heavy losses defending themselves. PSL says the aim was to force the tribes to terms and onto a reservation. Afterward the Kiowa Apache broke with the Kiowa and allied with the Cheyenne and Arapaho.
verbatim_quote: Kit Carson's brutal attack was an attempt to diminish the fighting capacity of the Kiowa and Comanche, forcing them to come to terms with the United States
sources_cited_by_source: Pafford 2017, Kit Carson's Last Fight, unpublished dissertation, 184 (endnote 11)
federal_account_contrast: Federal histories call it a battle. PSL frames it as coercion leading up to the 1865 and 1867 treaties.
map_implication: Add Adobe Walls 1864 as violence preceding the Little Arkansas (1865) and Medicine Lodge (1867) KCA treaties.
notes: The source calls it a battle and an 'attack', not a massacre; the category is the closest fit. Coordinates not given in the source.

instrument: Treaty of the Little Arkansas with Cheyenne, Arapaho and Apache 1865
summary: Apache chiefs Iron Shirt, Poor Bear, Old Fool Man, The Crow, The Wolf Sleeve and The Chief signed. The treaty dissolved the Apache confederation with the Kiowa-Comanche and joined them 'on an equal footing' with the Cheyenne-Arapaho. It promised Sand Creek reparations, 320-acre grants to band leaders and 160-acre grants to widows and orphans. PSL says it was never ratified, that $39,050 appropriated in 1866 was not delivered as promised, and that part was returned to the Treasury as 'surplus'.
verbatim_quote: the Interior Department gave some of the money to the tribes and, according to a modern legal assessment, 'returned the rest' to the Treasury as 'surplus.'
sources_cited_by_source: Colorado Encyclopedia, 'Little Arkansas Treaty' (endnotes 14-15, 18); treaty text (endnotes 16-17)
federal_account_contrast: Adds the Apache's distinct status, and the diversion of the reparation funds, to the treaty record.
map_implication: Record the 1865 Apache-Cheyenne-Arapaho treaty with its Sand Creek reparation lands as promised land that was never delivered, and the $39,050 diversion.
notes: CONTESTED: PSL says the Little Arkansas Treaty was 'never ratified'. The Cheyenne-Arapaho(-Apache) Little Arkansas treaty is generally recorded as ratified with Senate amendments (14 Stat. 703) that removed the reservation; the KC one is cited here as RIT 343, 14 Stat. 717. Check whether PSL means the reservation was never established. Page 86 wrongly says the 'Medicine Lodge Treaty of 1866' allocated the $39,050.

place: Arkansas Valley between SE Colorado and Kansas
summary: PSL infers that from 1865 to 1867 the Kiowa Apache lived with the Cheyenne and Arapaho in the Arkansas Valley between SE Colorado and Kansas, where the treaty gave them hunting rights.
verbatim_quote: It thus can be inferred that the Kiowa Apache were with the Cheyenne and Arapaho in the Arkansas Valley between southeastern Colorado and Kansas
sources_cited_by_source: Colorado Encyclopedia, 'Indigenous Treaties in Colorado' (endnote 19)
federal_account_contrast: Places the Apache in Colorado in the treaty era.
map_implication: Optional: Kiowa Apache presence/hunting layer in the Arkansas Valley, 1865-67, marked as inferred.
notes: The source says this is an inference.

instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge, Apache adhesion 1867
summary: Seven languages were spoken at the council. The Plains Apache had no proficient interpreter of their own; their speeches went through Arapaho by an Apache-speaking member of Little Raven's band. PSL questions how much the Apache headmen understood. Sherman ordered 50,000 rations for the council.
verbatim_quote: said Apache speeches were translated into Arapaho by an Apache-speaking member of Little Raven's tribe
sources_cited_by_source: Jones 1966, The Treaty of Medicine Lodge, 45, 104-108 (endnotes 22, 25-27)
federal_account_contrast: Kappler shows the Apache signing. PSL questions whether they gave informed consent.
map_implication: Flag the Apache adhesion to Medicine Lodge: 'no Apache-language interpreter; double translation via Arapaho'.
notes: The 50,000 rations is evidence of using rations as an inducement only by inference; PSL does not claim starvation duress. PSL gives the Apache signing date as 1867-10-25; the Apache adhesion is usually dated 1867-10-21 (15 Stat. 589). Needs checking.

place: Between Fort Cobb and Fort Sill, Indian Territory
summary: PSL says the treaty marked the 'unwilling loss, under duress' of the Apache nomadic life. The Apache settled between Fort Cobb and Fort Sill under Head Chief Pacer, and 'the tribes never received any of the annuities promised.' The population was about 325 by 1891.
verbatim_quote: the treaty marked the unwilling loss, under duress, of their traditional nomadic lifeways
sources_cited_by_source: McAllister & Anderson, Handbook of Texas (endnote 28) for the population
federal_account_contrast: Kappler implies the annuities were delivered under the treaty; PSL says none were received.
map_implication: Tag the Apache adhesion to Medicine Lodge as duress plus non-payment of annuities (single-source claim).
notes: The 'never received any' annuity claim is sweeping and has no cite; it needs verification.

summary: The Jerome Commission offered $2 million for about 2.5 million acres of 'surplus' land and 160 acres per person. The agent noted that the $210,000 biannual grass-lease payments from Texas cattlemen (1886) exceeded the 5% interest on $2 million. PSL says 160 acres could not sustain farming or ranching on the dry land.
verbatim_quote: offered $2 million for approximately 2.5 million acres of surplus land
sources_cited_by_source: Kracht, 'Kiowa-Comanche-Apache Opening', Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture (endnote 29)
federal_account_contrast: Shows the tribes were paid less than the land's lease income.
map_implication: Record the 1892 price of under $1/acre ($2M for about 2.5M acres) against $210K per 6 months in grass leases.
notes: The agent is named 'James F. Ranflett' (probably Randlett). 2.5M acres here vs 2,033,583 acres ceded in ICC Docket 32: the ICC figure is the ceded area; the reason for the gap is not explained.

summary: There are eleven recommendations to Colorado: (1) compensation for pain and suffering from illegal trespass; (2) compensation for water rights; (3) full compensation for the state's role in forced removal; (4) restoring unrestricted cultural use, hunting, fishing and plant gathering on all public lands; (5) payment for railway land, and return of abandoned rail lands; (6) GOCO funding access and sacred-site protection; (7) no property tax on enrolled members living in Colorado; (8) support for reopening the ICC settlement on appeal; (9) tuition waivers plus room and board; (10) a real-estate transaction fee for a permanent fund; (11) buffalo restoration.
verbatim_quote: It is recommended that the State of Colorado support the Kiowa, Comanche, and Apache Tribes of Oklahoma Nation in its efforts to have the Indian Claims Commission settlement opened for appeal.
sources_cited_by_source: Recommendation endnotes 1-11 (pp. 91-92)
federal_account_contrast: These are reparative proposals that go beyond the federal settlement.
map_implication: Optional 'TREC recommendations' panel on the KCA nation page.
notes: These are policy recommendations, not historical claims.

summary: Recommendation endnote 1 says the KCA lands were within the 1834 Act's Indian Country, so settlers were illegal intruders, and no agency corrected the occupation even when it knew it was illegal.
verbatim_quote: This violation was not corrected by any agency even when they knew the occupation was illegal.
sources_cited_by_source: 1834 Trade and Intercourse Act
federal_account_contrast: Treats settlement before cession as illegal trespass rather than a frontier.
map_implication: Consider a 'pre-cession illegal settlement' layer for SE Colorado KCA lands.

summary: Recommendation endnote 3 calls the forced removal an act of genocide and says Territorial Governor John Evans failed in his duties as Superintendent of Indian Affairs. It argues the state should be held liable and calls for a full investigation.
verbatim_quote: The forced removal was an act of genocide. Territorial Governor Evans failed in his duties as the Superintendent of Indian Affairs, and the state should be held liable for his actions.
sources_cited_by_source: None given
federal_account_contrast: Assigns responsibility to the territorial government, not only the federal one.
map_implication: Link Governor Evans's role to KCA removal from Colorado in the violations catalog.

instrument: Pacific Railroad Acts; Colorado School Fund grants
summary: Recommendation endnotes 5 and 9 say Colorado's economy grew from railroad land grants that gave KCA nothing, and that the School Fund received 4 million acres of Colorado land from which KCA students have not benefited.
verbatim_quote: The School Fund received 4 million acres of land in Colorado to support schools
sources_cited_by_source: None given
federal_account_contrast: Ties state trust land and railroad grants to Native land.
map_implication: Consider overlaying Colorado state school trust lands and railroad grant lands on KCA treaty areas.
notes: The 4 million acres figure needs checking against Colorado State Land Board records.

summary: Recommendation endnote 6 says Great Outdoors Colorado (GOCO) rules bar tribal nations from its funds, and that per the US Forest Service there are over 200 unprotected sacred sites.
verbatim_quote: According to the US Forest Service there are over 200 sacred sites that are not currently protected.
sources_cited_by_source: US Forest Service (no specific document)
notes: The 200-site figure has no specific source.

summary: PSL says the KCA homeland held the southern buffalo herd of about five million animals, the tribes' primary food source, worth about $46 billion today. It recommends buffalo restoration.
verbatim_quote: There were approximately five million buffalo in the southern herd. The value at today's price is calculated to be roughly 46,000,000,000 dollars.
sources_cited_by_source: None given (p.74 endnote 43 missing from chunk)
map_implication: Possibly note buffalo extermination as a resource taking enabling KCA cessions.
notes: This conflicts with the $48 billion figure on p.74.

summary: Recommendation endnote 7 argues KCA members living in Colorado have a reserved right not to pay state property tax because they still live in their homelands, and cites a 'protectorate clause' of the 1924 Citizenship Act.
verbatim_quote: have a reserved right not to pay state property taxes as they are still living within their homelands
sources_cited_by_source: Indian Citizenship Act 1924
notes: This is a legal theory that needs verification; the 1924 Act has no clause commonly known as a 'protectorate clause'.

instrument: Indian Reorganization Act 1934; Oklahoma Indian Welfare Act 1936
summary: Kiowa leaders opposed the IRA after meeting Collier on 1934-03-20, but Congress extended it to Oklahoma as the OIWA in 1936, which ended allotment. In the 1950s the Kiowa avoided termination by refusing to cooperate.
verbatim_quote: The Kiowa eventually avoided termination by refusing to cooperate with the federal government.
sources_cited_by_source: Kansapedia 'Kiowa' (endnotes 22-24)
notes: Context only. Also on pp.69-70: the Native American Church was incorporated in 1918 and the Kiowa Six enrolled at OU in 1928 (cultural context, no land implication).
